HOME.TITLE: Welcome to the ALICE Masterclass!
HOME.P1: The ALICE Collaboration has built a dedicated detector to exploit the unique physics potential of nucleus-nucleus collisions at LHC energies. Our aim is to study the physics of strongly interacting matter at the highest energy densities reached so far in the laboratory. In such condition, an extreme phase of matter - called the quark-gluon plasma - is formed.
HOME.P2: Our universe is thought to have been in such a primordial state for the first few millionths of a second after the Big Bang. The properties of such a phase are key issues for Quantum Chromo Dynamics, the understanding of confinement-deconfinement and chiral phase transitions.
HOME.P3: For this purpose, we are carrying out a comprehensive study of the hadrons, electrons, muons and photons produced in the collisions of heavy nuclei. ALICE is also studying proton-proton and proton-nucleus collisions both as a comparison with nucleus-nucleus collisions and in their own right.

INSTRUCTIONS_VISUAL_ANALYSIS.TITLE: Strange Particle Production
INSTRUCTIONS_VISUAL_ANALYSIS.SUBTITLE: Exercise 1: Visual inspection
INSTRUCTIONS_VISUAL_ANALYSIS.P1: The aim of the exercise is to search for strange particles produced from collisions at LHC and recorded by the ALICE experiment. Strange particles do not live long; they decay soon after their production. However, they live long enough to travel some distance (usually a few centimeters) from the interaction point (IP) from where they were produced (primary vertex). Their search is thus based on the identification of their decay products, which must originate from a common secondary vertex. Neutral strange particles, such as K0S and Λ, decay giving a characteristic decay pattern, called V0. The mother particle disappears some centimeters from the interaction point and two oppositely charged particles appear in its place, which are bent in opposite directions inside the magnetic field of the ALICE solenoid. In the following figure red tracks indicate positively charged particles; green tracks indicate negatively charged particles. The decays we will be looking for are:
INSTRUCTIONS_VISUAL_ANALYSIS.P2: We see that for a pion-pion the final state of the decay pattern is quasi-symmetric whereas in the pion-proton final state the radius of curvature of the proton is bigger than that of the pion: due to its higher mass, the proton carries most of the initial momentum.
INSTRUCTIONS_VISUAL_ANALYSIS.P3: We will also be looking for cascade decays of charged strange particles, such as the Ξ̅; this decays into π− Λ; the Λ then decays into π− and proton; the initial pion is characterized as a bachelor (single charged track) and is shown in purple. The search for V0s is based on the decay topology and the identification of the decay products; an additional confirmation of the particle identity is the calculation of its mass; this is done based on the information (mass and momentum) of the decay products.
INSTRUCTIONS_VISUAL_ANALYSIS.P4: In this exercise, you will determine the number of strange particles in 15 pp collisions at a collision energy of 7TeV particles can be identified through the topology of the their decays. When you select tracks from a V0 or Cascade, the relevant numbers (momentum in the form (px,py,pz) and mass) will automatically be sent to the Calculator interface, and the invariant mass for the current selected particles is calculated. Then you make a choice of particle type and click Add to include its mass in the graphs below.

INSTRUCTIONS_LARGE_SCALE_ANALYSIS.TITLE: Strange Particle Production
INSTRUCTIONS_LARGE_SCALE_ANALYSIS.SUBTITLE: Exercise 2: Large Scale Analysis
INSTRUCTIONS_LARGE_SCALE_ANALYSIS.P1: The event display is a powerful tool which helps check the quality of the data and their reconstruction and gives a “feeling” of what events look like. However,in real life data analysis is not done visually — that would be far too tedious and time-consuming. To analyse the millions of events that we collect daily at the LHC we run programs, and this is what you will do here, in order to look for V0s in a bigger event sample.
INSTRUCTIONS_LARGE_SCALE_ANALYSIS.P2: You will now analyse recordings from hundreds of events at once. You can see that the invariant mass is a continuous distribution – this is because the pairs of pions combined are random, not coming from a common secondary vertex and can give any value of mass. Most of them are background.
INSTRUCTIONS_LARGE_SCALE_ANALYSIS.P3: In order to find the number of particles of a certain type, for example K0S, you need to find the number of events in the peak after background subtraction. In order to fit a curve (second degree polynomial) to the background, you first choose the fit range using the slider. To fit a Gaussian distribution to the signal you also have to select the range of the peak. When you click on Fit, the fitted functions are superimposed on the histogram and you can check visually whether the fit is reasonable.If you think the fitted functions match the data well, you can push the Accept button. For the background subtraction the coefficients of the second degree polynomial are used; on the histogram; after clicking the Accept button you will get the total number of events in the peak, the number of background events and those which are signal.

INSTRUCTIONS_PARTICLE_PROPAGATION.TITLE: Particle Propagation in the Magnetic Field
INSTRUCTIONS_PARTICLE_PROPAGATION.SUBTITLE: How tracks curve through ALICE
INSTRUCTIONS_PARTICLE_PROPAGATION.P1: Two protons collide at the centre of the detector. The particles produced in the collision fly outward and are bent by the ALICE magnetic field (a solenoid around the barrel and a dipole around the muon arm), following a curved path described by the Lorentz force.
INSTRUCTIONS_PARTICLE_PROPAGATION.P2: Each track's trajectory is pre-computed once, ahead of time, using 4th-order Runge-Kutta (RK4) integration through the exact 3D magnetic field map (a Chebyshev polynomial model of the real ALICE field) — the browser never re-computes physics while you scrub or play the animation.
INSTRUCTIONS_PARTICLE_PROPAGATION.P3: Use the time slider to move through three phases: before the collision (the two protons approaching), the moment of collision, and afterwards (the produced particles propagating outward). Positively and negatively charged tracks curve in opposite directions; neutral tracks travel in a straight line.

PARTICLE_PROPAGATION.WELCOME_TITLE: Particle Propagation in the Magnetic Field
PARTICLE_PROPAGATION.WELCOME_BODY_1: Watch two protons collide at the centre of the ALICE detector, then see the produced particles propagate outward, bent by the real 3D magnetic field.
PARTICLE_PROPAGATION.WELCOME_BODY_2: Once you start the animation, trajectories are pre-computed using Runge-Kutta integration through the ALICE Chebyshev field map — this can take a moment for busy events.
PARTICLE_PROPAGATION.WELCOME_BODY_3: Afterwards, use the time slider to scrub freely through the collision and the propagation that follows.
